web_evidence.title: Excerpt from 'A Mercy'
web_evidence.note: A sustained Chapter One excerpt credited to Knopf shows Florens narrating as I and addressing the blacksmith as you; it also supplies context for several clipped Goodreads quotations.

web_evidence.title: Narrative Strategies in Toni Morrison's A Mercy
web_evidence.note: Ksenija Kondali's scholarly article explicitly says Florens's recurring sections use first-person present narration while the intervening sections use third-person free-indirect narration in the past.

web_evidence.title: The Powerful Writing Strategies of Assia Djebar and Toni Morrison: Differentiation of the Depictions of Otherness Through Literature
web_evidence.note: Sanne Boersma's Utrecht University MA thesis describes A Mercy as multilayered: most characters' stories are in third person, while Florens's story is in first person.

web_evidence.title: A Mercy Study Guide
web_evidence.note: Its explicit narrator overview says the novel switches between first-person and third-person narration, identifies Florens and her mother as the first-person narrators, and identifies the other character narratives as third person.

web_evidence.title: Characters and Communities in A Mercy
web_evidence.note: Chicago Public Library maps Florens's recurring address chapters, the intervening chapters centered on Jacob, Lina, Rebekka, Sorrow, Willard and Scully, and the final chapter addressed by Florens's mother, corroborating that these are sustained sections rather than isolated insertions.

person_note: The novel contains sustained base sections in different grammatical persons. Florens repeatedly narrates in first person while addressing the blacksmith, and Florens's mother supplies another sustained first-person section at the end; multiple first-person narrators alone would still count as FIRST. However, those chapters alternate with sustained third-person free-indirect sections centered on Jacob, Lina, Rebekka, Sorrow, Willard, and Scully, so the book-level label is ALTERNATING. Several quotes bucketed as dialogue are actually parts of Florens's or her mother's constitutive address and were used as first-person evidence without changing their upstream buckets; the blacksmith's rebuke remains local speech. Goodreads supplies repeated first- and third-person passages, and multiple scholarly or explicit whole-book sources independently confirm the structure. The main residual uncertainty is attribution of a few clipped individual quotations, not the book-level alternation.
